question: Under RPL Section 442(2), a broker handling a cooperative apartment or homeowners association property transaction is permitted a specific compensation exception. What does it allow?
choice_a: Compensating individuals whose primary business lies outside real estate, in addition to licensed salespersons, licensed brokers, and licensed out-of-state professionals
choice_b: Paying an unlimited commission to any unlicensed person regardless of the type of property involved
choice_c: Waiving the license requirement entirely for cooperative and homeowners association transactions
choice_d: Charging a commission rate fixed by the cooperative board rather than negotiated with the client
explanation: RPL Section 442(2) creates a narrow, transaction-type-specific exception: for cooperative or homeowners association property, a broker may compensate individuals whose primary business is outside the real estate field, in addition to the licensed salespersons/brokers otherwise permitted under Section 442(1) -- a departure from the general prohibition on paying unlicensed parties.
source_note: RPL Article 12-A, Section 442(2) (Splitting commissions -- cooperative/HOA exception)

question: Under RPL Section 442(2)'s general restriction, may a broker pay a portion of a commission directly to a transaction party (the buyer, seller, landlord, or tenant)?
choice_a: A broker may offer a compensation portion to the buyer, seller, landlord, or tenant, but not as a reward tied to performing licensed brokerage activities
choice_b: No, under no circumstances may any payment ever reach a transaction party
choice_c: Yes, without any restriction whatsoever on the amount or purpose
choice_d: Only the buyer, never the seller, may ever receive any portion of a commission
explanation: Section 442(2) permits a broker to offer a compensation portion to a party to the transaction itself (such as a buyer rebate), but bars structuring that payment as a reward for performing what would otherwise be licensed brokerage activity -- distinguishing a permissible rebate from an improper payment for unlicensed brokerage work.
source_note: RPL Article 12-A, Section 442(2) (general restriction on paying transaction parties)

question: Under RPL Section 442-l, a broker or salesperson is barred from demanding or receiving a referral fee for finding a seller once what event has occurred?
choice_a: A bona fide listing agreement has already been signed
choice_b: The property has been on the market for at least 90 days
choice_c: The seller has changed real estate attorneys
choice_d: The broker has advertised the property on at least three platforms
explanation: RPL Section 442-l prohibits demanding or accepting a referral fee tied to finding a seller after a bona fide listing agreement for that seller has already been signed -- an 'after-the-fact' referral is barred because the referral no longer serves any real matchmaking function once the listing relationship already exists.
source_note: RPL Article 12-A, Section 442-l (After-the-fact referral fees -- post-listing referrals)

question: Under RPL Section 442-l, a broker or salesperson is similarly barred from demanding or receiving a referral fee for finding a buyer once what event has occurred?
choice_a: A bona fide offer to purchase has already been accepted
choice_b: The buyer has attended a single open house
choice_c: The buyer has obtained a mortgage pre-qualification letter
choice_d: More than one broker has shown the buyer a property
explanation: Mirroring the post-listing rule, Section 442-l bars an after-the-fact referral fee for 'finding' a buyer once a bona fide offer to purchase from that buyer has already been accepted -- again targeting fees for a referral that no longer serves any genuine matchmaking purpose.
source_note: RPL Article 12-A, Section 442-l (After-the-fact referral fees -- post-offer referrals)

question: Under RPL Section 442-l, what third after-the-fact referral scenario is also prohibited, alongside the post-listing and post-accepted-offer scenarios?
choice_a: A referral fee for finding a property after a bona fide buyer's agency agreement has already been signed
choice_b: A referral fee for finding a title insurance company at any point in the transaction
choice_c: A referral fee paid before any agreement of any kind exists
choice_d: A referral fee involving a cooperative apartment specifically
explanation: Section 442-l's third prohibited scenario bars a referral fee for finding a property after a bona fide buyer's agency agreement has already been signed -- rounding out the statute's targeting of referral fees demanded or paid only after the underlying relationship or transaction milestone has already been locked in.
source_note: RPL Article 12-A, Section 442-l (After-the-fact referral fees -- post-buyer's-agency-agreement referrals)

question: Under RPL Section 442-l, is there any exception that would allow a referral fee in one of the three otherwise-prohibited after-the-fact scenarios?
choice_a: Yes -- payment may still be made where reasonable cause for the compensation exists
choice_b: No -- the prohibition is absolute with no exception under any circumstance
choice_c: Yes, but only if the referral fee is under $50
choice_d: Yes, but only for commercial transactions, never residential
explanation: Section 442-l is not an absolute bar -- it allows for payment where reasonable cause for the compensation exists, giving some flexibility for legitimate compensation arrangements that happen to arise after the specified milestone, while still targeting fees demanded purely because the deal has already effectively closed.

question: Under RPL Section 442-l, how is a violation of the after-the-fact referral fee prohibition additionally characterized under New York consumer-protection law?
choice_a: As a deceptive act or practice within the meaning of General Business Law Section 349
choice_b: As an antitrust violation under the federal Sherman Act exclusively
choice_c: As a violation with no connection to any other body of law
choice_d: As a tax evasion offense under the Internal Revenue Code
explanation: Section 442-l expressly ties a violation of its after-the-fact referral fee prohibition to General Business Law Section 349's deceptive-acts-and-practices standard, layering a separate consumer-protection enforcement avenue on top of Article 12-A's own licensing-discipline framework.
source_note: RPL Article 12-A, Section 442-l; General Business Law Section 349 (cross-reference)

question: Under 19 NYCRR Section 175.7, a real estate broker who wishes to receive compensation from more than one party in the same transaction must first obtain what?
choice_a: The full knowledge and consent of the broker's client
choice_b: Nothing further -- dual compensation is always permitted without any disclosure
choice_c: A separate license specifically authorizing dual compensation
choice_d: Approval from the buyer's mortgage lender only
explanation: 19 NYCRR Section 175.7 requires that a broker make clear which party they represent, and prohibits receiving compensation from more than one party in the transaction except with the full knowledge and consent of the broker's client -- a compensation-focused counterpart to the broader agency-disclosure rules under RPL Section 443.

question: A broker representing the seller quietly accepts an additional payment from the buyer for 'expediting' the deal, without telling the seller. Under 19 NYCRR Section 175.7, is this compliant?
choice_a: No -- receiving compensation from more than one party without the client's full knowledge and consent violates Section 175.7, regardless of how the extra payment is characterized
choice_b: Yes, as long as the extra payment is less than the broker's commission from the seller
choice_c: Yes, because buyers are always free to pay a broker anything they wish
choice_d: Yes, provided the buyer signs a receipt for the payment
explanation: Accepting undisclosed compensation from the buyer while representing the seller is exactly the conflict-of-interest scenario Section 175.7 is designed to prevent -- the broker's client (the seller) must have full knowledge and give consent before the broker may accept payment from the other side, regardless of what the payment is labeled.

question: Under 19 NYCRR Section 175.24, a broker offering an exclusive residential listing agreement must attach a written explanation distinguishing between which two listing types?
choice_a: Exclusive right to sell and exclusive agency
choice_b: Net listing and open listing only
choice_c: Buyer's agency and dual agency only
explanation: 19 NYCRR Section 175.24 requires an exclusive residential listing agreement to be accompanied by a written explanation -- in minimum 6-point type, signed or initialed by the homeowner -- distinguishing an 'exclusive right to sell' listing (commission owed regardless of who finds the buyer) from an 'exclusive agency' listing (commission owed only if another broker finds the buyer).
source_note: 19 NYCRR Section 175.24 (Exclusive residential listings -- required disclosure)

question: Under 19 NYCRR Section 175.24, if a broker who belongs to a multiple listing service obtains an exclusive residential listing, what option must the homeowner be given regarding how purchase offers are submitted?
choice_a: The option to have offers submitted through either the listing broker or the selling (cooperating) broker
choice_b: No option at all -- all offers must go exclusively through the listing broker with no alternative
choice_c: The option to have offers submitted only through DOS directly
choice_d: The option to require offers be submitted only in cash, with no financed offers permitted
explanation: Section 175.24 requires that, when the listing broker is an MLS member, the exclusive listing agreement give the homeowner the option to have purchase offers submitted through either the listing broker or the broker who procured the buyer -- preventing a listing broker from being the sole conduit for offers on an MLS-listed exclusive.
source_note: 19 NYCRR Section 175.24 (Exclusive residential listings -- MLS offer-submission option)

question: A brokerage's listing agreement form fails to include the required 6-point-type explanation distinguishing exclusive right to sell from exclusive agency, and the homeowner signs without that explanation. What compliance problem results under 19 NYCRR Section 175.24?
choice_a: The listing agreement fails to satisfy Section 175.24's disclosure requirement, exposing the broker to potential discipline regardless of which listing type was actually intended
choice_b: There is no problem, since the disclosure requirement is purely optional guidance with no compliance consequence
choice_c: There is no problem as long as the commission rate itself was properly disclosed
choice_d: The listing agreement is automatically converted into an open listing by operation of law
explanation: Section 175.24 makes the written, signed-or-initialed explanation of exclusive right to sell versus exclusive agency a required part of an exclusive residential listing agreement -- omitting it is a recordkeeping and disclosure violation exposing the broker to discipline, independent of which listing type the parties actually intended to use.

question: How do RPL Section 442-l's after-the-fact referral fee restrictions relate to RPL Section 442's general anti-unlicensed-compensation rule discussed earlier in this bucket?
choice_a: Section 442-l is a narrower, timing-based restriction targeting a specific category of referral fee regardless of the recipient's license status, while Section 442's core concern is compensating an unlicensed party for performing licensed services -- they address related but analytically distinct commission-integrity concerns
choice_b: The two sections are entirely identical and were both enacted in the same year with the same text
choice_c: Section 442-l completely repealed Section 442's unlicensed-compensation prohibition
choice_d: Section 442-l applies only to salespersons, and Section 442 applies only to brokers, with zero overlap in scope
explanation: Section 442's core concern is paying an unlicensed party for what amounts to licensed brokerage work, while Section 442-l is a narrower, timing-focused rule barring referral fees demanded only after a listing, offer, or buyer's agency agreement is already locked in -- a licensed broker could violate 442-l even though no unlicensed-party issue under Section 442 is present at all.
